headline: AI is getting more capable and more expensive at the same time. We work on the second half of that sentence.
intro: Reading a scan, drafting a summary, steering an experiment: every useful thing a model does costs electricity, hardware, and time. Those costs decide who gets to use it. A system that demands a rack of accelerators serves the institutions that can afford a rack of accelerators, while a system that fits on a wearable serves a patient at home. PEARL moves the line between those two worlds. We build the runtimes, memory systems, schedulers, and compilers that bring demanding computation within reach of the hardware people already have.
closing: Efficiency is an access question. Speed and cost are never the point on their own; they decide whether a capability stays in a datacenter or reaches a clinic, a classroom, a field station, a phone.

thrusts.title: Making AI affordable to run
thrusts.stake: Serving a model costs more than training it. That is where the dollars and the electricity go.
thrusts.blurb: Training happens once. Serving happens a billion times. We rebuild the serving stack so the same hardware answers many more questions: overlapping CPU and GPU work instead of letting either idle, restructuring how the KV cache is stored and shared, discarding tokens that do not change the output, and setting numerical precision per layer and per timestep rather than once for the whole model.
highlights: APEX — asynchronous CPU–GPU execution that serves online LLM inference on GPUs too small for the model
dLLM-Serve — closing the memory gap in diffusion language model serving
HiRED — attention-guided token dropping for high-resolution vision–language models
DiffPro — joint timestep and layer-wise precision optimization for diffusion inference
HydraCache — long-context prefill parallelization via distributed cache blending

thrusts.title: Putting intelligence where people are
thrusts.stake: Some data should never leave the device that measured it. Some decisions cannot wait for a round trip.
thrusts.blurb: A wearable flags an arrhythmia. A camera watches a production line. A base station reallocates spectrum. Each needs an answer in milliseconds, often over an unreliable network, and frequently from data too sensitive to send anywhere at all. We work out how to divide a model across the device, the edge server, and the cloud: what to quantize, what to speculate, what to transmit. The intelligence runs next to the person, and the expensive machinery runs only when it earns its place.
highlights: SWEET — workload-balanced edge inference via quantization and partitioning (NSF, with QUB and UCD)
SLED and WISP — speculative LLM decoding and SLO-aware batching at the edge
Polymorph — energy-efficient video classification on embedded devices
MARVEL — custom RISC-V extensions generated for a whole class of lightweight AI models
Accelerating transformer inference on RISC-V for edge AI
O-RAN slicing — scaling and placing edge servers for next-generation wireless

thrusts.title: Getting more out of the hardware that already exists
thrusts.stake: Accelerators are scarce and expensive. Most of them sit idle.
thrusts.blurb: A GPU handed to a single tenant runs at half capacity. A dataset that overflows fast memory drags an entire job down to the speed of the slowest tier. Buying more hardware fixes neither, because both are scheduling and memory-management failures rather than shortages. We build the mechanisms that let several workloads share one accelerator safely, predict which pages a program will need before it stalls, and place data across memory tiers without asking the programmer to think about it.
highlights: ParvaGPU — spatial GPU sharing for large-scale DNN inference in the cloud
Stride-aware page prefetching for GPU unified memory via Markov prediction
Memory tiering inside the Python virtual machine
Application-attuned memory management for containerized HPC workflows

thrusts.title: Teaching machines to make scientific code fast
thrusts.stake: Most scientific software runs well below what its hardware allows. Tuning it is a specialist skill, and specialists are scarce.
thrusts.blurb: A climate model or a genomics pipeline is written by a domain scientist, not a performance engineer, and the distance between the two is often an order of magnitude in runtime. We build multi-agent systems that read the code, propose transformations, measure what happens, and keep only the changes that survive measurement. Trusting a machine-written optimization takes benchmarks and guardrails, so we build those alongside the agents. Undergraduate researchers lead much of this work.
highlights: MARCO — multi-agent code optimization for high-performance computing
FACT — compositional CUDA kernel synthesis grounded in CUTLASS C++
LLM-guided runtime parameter tuning for energy-efficient inference
AI-driven autonomous experimentation for turbulent flows
Parallel Islands — teaching parallel computing through a video game

thrusts.title: Making it hold up, and making it cheap to run
thrusts.stake: A system that returns a wrong answer without warning, or quietly consumes a power budget, is worse than one that fails outright.
thrusts.blurb: At scale, hardware faults stop being hypothetical and energy stops being an afterthought. We measure where the joules go, stage by stage and instruction by instruction, then build recovery mechanisms that let a long computation survive a failure without restarting from zero. The aim is a system whose cost and correctness you can reason about before committing a month of machine time to it.
highlights: Modality inflation — energy characterization of multimodal LLM inference
Power Log'n'Roll — power-efficient localized rollback for MPI applications
SAFIRE — compiler-driven parallel fault injection (with LLNL)
Dynamic precision iterative refinement
